segments.translation: It is better now! If I would’ve brought a ladder, I would’ve heard good the first time!

segments.text: ᎮᏍᏗᏍ ᏌᎶᎳ ᏱᏍᏕᎵᏍᎨᏍᏗ ᎯᎠ. ᎯᏅ Guy Soldier ᏓᏩᏙ JayᎢ ᏂᏛᎩᎶᏒ; ᏍᏓᏅᏔᏛ ᎤᎾ JayᎢ ᎨᎲ?

segments.translation: Jay! Yeah, Dlaygv.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Yeah and uh… ᎾᎿ ᏗᏩᏛᏏᏙᎸ ᏜᏱᎬ.
segments.transliteration: Yeah and uh… nahna diwadvsidolv dlayigv.
segments.translation: Yeah and uh… That is where I grew up. Dlaygv.

segments.translation: Dlaygv.

segments.text: ᎯᏅ ᏓᏍᏛᏯᏛᏛᎮᏢᏂ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎤᏃᏪᎸ ᏍᏊ ᏛᎬᏛᏂ.

segments.translation: Yes ok.

segments.translation: Charley McCoy… yeah. What about you?

segments.translation: What?

segments.translation: So, you were born there?

segments.translation: No, I was born in Claremore.

segments.translation: Oh, Claremore.

segments.translation: Yeah, Claremore was where I was born.

segments.translation: What?

segments.translation: Yeah, I have heard of it.

segments.translation: It is pretty far from here.

segments.text: Yeah, mm hm yeah, yeah, ᎥᎲ ᏂᎾᎭ?

segments.text: Ꮎ Caney Creek ᎾᎠ ᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ Ꮲ ᏅᎩ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᎢᎪᎯᏓ ᎣᎦᏕᏅ ᎤᎾ ᏃᏭᏅ ᎦᏙ ᏣᏥᎩᎡᎳ ᎡᎵᏌ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮎ lake ᏧᎩᎡᎸ ᎣᎩᎾᎷᏒ Babo Ꮓ ᏩᏩᏛᏒ ᎤᎾ ᎦᏚᏑᏬ ᏗᏝ Babo ᎠᏃᏎᎰ ᎤᎾ ᏩᏩᏛᏒᏃ

segments.translation: It was near Caney Creek. About four years we lived there. And then my grandmother got her land taken away. The lake took it away [dammed to form a reservoir—Lake Tenkiller] We went up the hill. And I grew up in Barber, just up above [Caney Creek, they call it Babo. And that is where I grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ Old Euchi ᎠᏩᏕᏅ ᏍᏊ ᎦᏙ ᏥᎪᎩᎩᎡᎳ Ꮓ ᎠᎹᏯᏃ

segments.translation: I also was born in old Eucha, they took our land away, it is a lake there now. [Lake Eucha formed by damming, submerged this Cherokee community land in 1952.]

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛ ᏄᎵᏍᏓᏁᎸᏃ ᎠᎹᏯ Tenkiller Lake ᎤᎩᏒ ᎦᏙ ᎠᏯ ᎾᏍᏊ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏧᎶᎪᏗ ᎤᏬᏢᏒ ᏃᏅ Dry CreekᏃ ᎡᎾ Wildlife Department ᏥᎬᏩᎩᎡᎳ

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I’ll be…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, ok yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That has happened to a lot of us, hasn’t it?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: A lot!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎦᏙ ᎡᎩᎩᎡᎳ. ᏗᎨᎬ ᏍᏊ ᏍᎩ ᏥᏄᏅᎵᏍᏓᏁᎸ ᏗᎨᎬ ᏗᏝ ᎨᏥᎩᎡᎳ ᎦᏙ yeah ᏃᎮᏂ ᏥᏈᏍᏓ ᏱᎩᎮ ᎦᏙ ᏙᎲ ᏍᎩ ᏁᎬᏁᎸᎾ ᏱᎨᎮ

segments.translation: We have had our land taken, where I come from, that is what happened to them where I am from. They got their land taken away, yeah; we could’ve had lots of land if they didn’t do that to us.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: yeah, ᎣᏍᏕ ᏱᏄᏅᏛᏁ ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᎪᎯᏴᏥᎦ ᏝᎾ ᎦᏓ ᏳᏂᎭ ᎠᎾᏙᎵᏍᎦ ᎯᎸᏍᎦ ᏯᏍᎪᎯᏥᏆ ᏏᏅᏓ ᎠᎾᏈᏱᏍᎦ

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah!

segments.translation: It really shouldn’t have been like that.

segments.translation: I worked at a few different places when I was a young man. I started working at Cookson Store for a while. George Stratton was the name of the owner. His wife's name was Helen, they were good people, very friendly. I worked there for a while and then that big water came and they closed it, then they started building on the water. Boat docks they called them, for boats, and then someone from Ft. Smith came and started building some like that there at Cookson Bend was the name there. He found out I was working, and he came to Cookson, “I will pay you more if you help me build those boat docks,” he told me. “We will see what happens, I help my friend out here,” I told him. “We will talk about it. I can't go with you right away. If I can give him a week or two weeks' notice that I am going to quit, then I will go,” I told him and he agreed so that is what I did and went to build where they put boats, boat docks. He had a little store, and I worked there and then I worked there for about two years and that store owner at Cookson, his son, a young man, he was building all the way around that lake you would call it. “Did you build those building at the lake?” he said. “Yeah, I helped,” I told him. “I am not building on the water I am building on the mountain,” he told me. “I want you to help me,” he said. “This really is my house where I walk and work,” I told him. “Don’t think anything. No mistake, I can meet here at the store and leave from here in the mornings. We will go around building. A meeting place will be at Cookson,” he said. “I will give him a week notice to find someone else to help him, I can't just quit,” I told him. So, I went and helped him for a week at a time, sometimes for longer. I was building around there on the water and then when we finished all those houses around the lake there is just a few buildings we did not build. And when we finished there, St. Claire Lime Company, Sallisaw then they called me and said you can help us. I have never made white dust before.“ You will not be making any, you can just watch the workers. If they are doing good or not, you will be sitting up high. There are stairs, you can sit up high on the second step, you can show them what to do,” he told me. “I don’t know if I can show them what to do, I have never done that before. I have never made lime before,” I told them. We are going to tell you what to do, you just have to watch the meters and when you watch the meters there were several of them and when you watch the meters, they got to hold at a certain degree. All 24 hours, they can't go up, they can't go down, they got to stay right there. “I can do that,” I told him. “I know you can do it,” that boss told me. Then I started there and worked for a long time. I was working there when I went into the Army, when I got out and finished the Army, where did I start then?

segments.transliteration: Pete Foster dudov agidoda unagi dv dudov tsalagi gvdvnv etsi na gehv yo Sally Hooper sali ini dudov edoda nv vian nidvyunigida etsi no na babo udvsidolv asena neladv yinvda gvge gehv dunagvlenvhv sgino elisa tsigehv no osdatlawasdvnitlv aya
segments.translation: Pete Foster was his English name Unegi was his name in Cherokee. My Mom was Sally Hooper and Sali was her name. Dad was from Vian, and Mom was from Barber where she grew up. But I was 18 months old when they separated, we came to live with my grandmother.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then she scolded you?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏍᎩᏛᏃ, ᏙᏳ ᏍᏊ ᎦᏙᏛ ᏴᏗ ᎢᎦ ᎤᏍᎦᎮᏗ ᏧᏁᏟᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏍᏊ ᏍᎩᎾᎾ ᎠᏂ strict ᏥᏓᏃᎮ ᏳᏍᏗ
segments.transliteration: vv sgidvno, doyu squu gadodv yvdi iga usgahedi tsunetlidi gehv squu sginana ani strict tsidanohe yusdi
segments.translation: Yeah, then she did. And she really was, what would you say? She was a strong Christian, she was. She was what they call strict.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ Ꮫ ᏍᏊ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏂᎪᎳ ᏣᎦᏐᎮᎲ. ᏙᏛᏩᏍᎬ ᏒᎾᎴ ᏱᎦ ᏧᏂᎵᎳᏫᏍᏗ ᎮᎾ
segments.transliteration: aya dv squu agayvlige nigola tsagasohehv. dodvwasgv svnale yiga tsunililawisdi hena
segments.translation: Me too, that old lady was always getting on to me. Sunday morning, “Go to church!”

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: I too have been scolded about some things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎾᎾᎭ ᏧᏂᏴᏫᏗ ᏙᎤᏍᏗ ᏗᏍᏗᏴᏫᏗ ᏂᎯ? Ꮎ clan ᏣᎾᏗᎰ
segments.transliteration: nanaha tsuniyvwidi dousdi disdiyvwidi nihi? na clan tsanadiho
segments.translation: What about clans, what are y’all's clans, what they call clans.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Ꭰ ᎠᏂᏌᎰᏂ Ꮫ ᏧᏂᏴᏫᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏯ ᏗᎩᎬᏴᎵᎨ
segments.transliteration: a anisahoni dv tsuniyvwidi gehv aya digigvyvlige
segments.translation: Yeah, Anisvhonii (Blue) was my parent's clan.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Anisahoni.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏔ Ꮓ ᏳᏍᏗ Ꮓ ᏙᏛ ᏴᏛᎩᏃ ᏴᏁᏟᏗ?
segments.transliteration: tla yawanvta no yusdi no dodv yvdvgino yvnetlidi?
segments.translation: I don’t know what you would do to translate that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like what.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Anisahoni…

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᏄᏍᏓ ᎠᎦᏛᎦᏅ ᏲᎾ ᎤᏠᏯᏍᏓ ᎲᏍᏊ ᏯᏩᎾᏔ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏠᏯᏍᏗᏍᎬ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏲᎾ ᎤᏠᏯᏍᏗ ᏢᏍᏊ ᏯᏩᎾᏘ ᎤᏍᏓ ᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: nusda agadvganv yona utloyasda hvsquu yawanata usdi utloyasdisgv aseno yona utloyasdi tlvsquu yawanati usda gehv
segments.translation: From what I have heard, Bear is involved but I don’t know how it’s involved. Bear is involved, but I don’t know how that is.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And you, what is your clan?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Anitsisqua (Bird)

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Anitsisqua (Bird)

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎾᎾᎲ ᏗᏣᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮩ ᏧᎾᏙᎩᏗ ᎨᎮ ᏧᏂᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ?
segments.transliteration: nanahv ditsagayvlige tsigehv do tsunadogidi gehe tsunigayvlige sgina?
segments.translation: Anitsisqua. Oh ok yeah. What about your parents? What were their parents’ names?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏗᏣᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏴᏛᏂ your mom and dad Ꮩ ᏧᎾᏙᎢᏗ ᎨᎮ ᏧᏂᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ?
segments.transliteration: ditsagvyvlige tsigehv yvdvni your mom and dad do tsunadoidi gehe tsunigvyvlige sgina?
segments.translation: Your parents. Like, for instance, your mom and dad. What was their parent’s names?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Their parents… What was my dad's dad’s name?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Alec McCoy.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Yeah, Alec McCoy ᏚᏙᎥ ᎤᏙᏓ ᎤᏥᏅ let’s see Martha Glory ᏚᏙᎥ ᎡᏥᏃ ᎤᏙᏓ Ꮭ ᏥᏲᎵᎦ ᏱᎨᎮ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏔ Ꮲ ᏨᏛᎦᏅ ᏱᎨᎮ ᏚᏙᎥ?
segments.transliteration: Yeah, Alec McCoy dudov udoda utsinv let’s see Martha Glory dudov etsino udoda tla tsiyoliga yigehe tla yawanvta tlv tsvdvganv yigehe dudov?
segments.translation: Yeah, Alec McCoy was his name, and his mom, let's see… Martha Glory was her name. My mom’s dad, I didn’t know him. I don’t know. You didn’t hear what his name was?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: No, I haven’t heard of it.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: But they were all full natives.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᏍᎩᎾᎾ ᎡᎵᎩ ᏣᏗᏍᎬ ᎦᏅᎯᏗᏍ ᎤᏍᏘᎩ ᏥᎨᏒ ᏥᏍ ᏙᎨ ᏣᏃᎮᎰ curly hair
segments.transliteration: sginana eligi tsadisgv ganvhidis ustigi tsigesv tsis doge tsanoheho curly hair
segments.translation: That Alec you said, did he have long hair? What do they say for curly hair?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Curly.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᎤᎵᏥᏍᏆᏁᏗ ᎦᏅᎯᏓ ᎢᎧ ᎤᏍᏗᎦ ᏥᎨᏒ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏔᎯᏍᏓ ᎡᎵᎦ ᏥᎨᏒ
segments.transliteration: ulitsisquanedi ganvhida ika usdiga tsigesv sgina utahisda eliga tsigesv
segments.translation: Curly! He had long hair, didn’t he? That old man, the late Alec.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Long hair, his hair was long.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Long hair…

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏍᎩᎾᎾ ᎤᏛᎯᏍᏗ ᎡᎵᎦ McCoy ᎠᎩᎪᎲ Ꮎ ᏗᏓᏟᎶᏍᏛᏅ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏛᎯᏍᏓ ᎦᏅᎯᏓ ᎤᏍᏗᎦ ᎤᎵᏥᏍᏆᏁᏓ ᏥᎨᏒ ᎤᏍᏗᎦ ᏍᎩᏍ?
segments.transliteration: vv sginana udvhisdi eliga McCoy agigohv na didatlilosdvnv sgina udvhisda ganvhida usdiga ulitsisquaneda tsigesv usdiga sgis?
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah that old man Alec McCoy. I have seen a picture of that old man. He had long and curly hair, is that him?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛᎮ ᎠᎮ ᎨᎮ, ᏱᎦᏓᏅᏖᏍᎨ ᏱᏗᎩᏫᏛᎮ ᏗᎨᎬᏟᎶᏍᏛᏅ ᏓᎩ
segments.transliteration: sgidvhe ahe gehe, yigadanvtesge yidigiwidvhe digegvtlilosdvnv dagi
segments.translation: I guess it was him. If I was thinking I would have brought a picture of him.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, yeah…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? What was their names?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎡᏙᏓᏛ ᎤᏙᏓ ᎤᏥᏅ James Foster ᏚᏙᎥ ᎤᏙᏓ ᎤᏥᏃ Annie, Annie Bearpaw ᎨᎲ maiden name ᏍᏊ ᏂᎦᏗ ᎠᏂᎧᎵ ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: edodadv udoda utsinv James Foster dudov udoda utsino Annie, Annie Bearpaw gehv maiden name squu nigadi anikali aniyvwiya gehv
segments.translation: My dad’s dad and mom, James Foster was my grandfather's name, and his mom was Annie. Bearpaw was her maiden name. They were all full natives.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did they come from?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: Vian ᏕᏝ ᎡᏥᏏ ᏗᏝ ᎨᎲ Ꮓ ᎤᏥ ᎵᏗ ᎠᏳᎢᏂ Lydia Swimmer ᏧᏙᎢᏗ ᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: Vian detla etsisi ditla gehv no utsi lidi ayuini Lydia Swimmer tsudoidi gehv
segments.translation: From towards Vian, yeah towards Vian. And on my mom's side her mom was Lydia Swimmer and her father was Jack Hooper.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh ok.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎤᏙᏗᏃ jack hooper, ᏤᎩ ᎠᏙᎯᏍᎦ ᏣᏃᎮᎲ
segments.transliteration: udodino jack hooper, tsegi adohisga tsanohehv
segments.translation: Yeah, Jack Atohisgi [He hoops] they used to call him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did they use to call him?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Atohisgi [He hoops].

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎤᎾᎾ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏚᎶᎨᏒ ᏭᎵᏍᏛ ᏚᏂᎶᎨᏒ ᎡᏚᏓ ᎤᎾᎵᎪ ᎠᏏᎾ ᏚᏙᎥ ᎤᎾ ᏭᎵᏍᏛ ᏚᎵᏍᎪᏝᏓᏁᎸ ᎠᏂᏳᏫᏯ Ꮎ ᎤᏛᎯᏍᏓ ᎠᏏᎾ ᏚᏙᎥ john bolin ᎤᎾ ᏭᎵᏍᏓ ᏚᎵᏍᎪᏢᏓᏁᎸ Cherokee nation ᎠᎮ ᎨᎮ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏁᏆᏍᏗ ᎤᎾ ᎦᏓ ᎤᎲ Ꮎ ᎤᏛᎯᏍᏓ ᎡᏚᏓ ᎤᎲ ᎦᏓ and ᏝᏍᏊ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᎾᏈᏗ ᏝᏍᏊ ᎸᎯᏳ ᏳᎾᏈᏴᎮ ᎠᏓᏁᎳ ᎤᎾ
segments.transliteration: unana edoda dulogesv wulisdv dunilogesv eduda unaligo asina dudov una wulisdv dulisgotladanelv aniyuwiya na udvhisda asina dudov john bolin una wulisda dulisgotlvdanelv Cherokee nation ahe gehe nahiyu tsunadelaquasdi unanequasdi una gada uhv na udvhisda eduda uhv gada and tlasquu gohusdi unaquidi tlasquu lvhiyu yunaquiyvhe adanela una
segments.translation: At the end of my father's field, where they had the fields, him and my grandpa, Asin was his name. There, at the end, he let the natives... Asen was that old man's name John Bolin. There on the end, he let them, I guess it was Cherokee Nation at the time, they built a school on that old man's land, my grandpa’s land. They never paid anything. That building is still there. That is where I went to school.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: yeah

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Ꭵ, ᎤᎾ ᎮᏂ ᏓᏩᏕᎳᏆᎥ ᎠᏫᏴ ᎠᏩᏂᎩᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏕᎦᏕᎳᏆᎡᎦ ᎡᎳᏗ ᎬᏂᎨᏒᏭ ᎤᎾᏭ ᎠᏩᏛᏒ indian day ᏚᏙᎥ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᏨᏛᎦᏅ Ꭾ? indian day Ꮟ ᎠᏓᏁᎷ that old school ᎾᏅ ᏗᎾᏓᏲᎲᏍᎩ ᎤᎾᏁᎸᏗᏍᏗ ᎠᏓᏁᎷ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏧᏂᎳᏫᏍᏗ Ꮓ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ Ꮎ ᏧᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᏗ ᏄᎵᏍᏛᏅ dry creek church ᎠᏃᏎᎰ ᏲᏎᏭᎾ ᏄᏂᏁᏟᏴᏓ ᏱᎨᎮ ᏚᏙᎥ ᏁᎸᎩ indian day church ᏱᏚᏙᎡ indian day school ᎢᎾ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: v, una heni dawadelaquav awiyv awanigisdi gehv degadelaquaega eladi gvnigesvwu unawu awadvsv indian day dudov tsunadelaquasdi tsvdvganv he? indian day si adanelu that old school nanv dinadayohvsgi unanelvdisdi adanelu aseno tsunilawisdi no gohiyv tsiga na tsunadelaquasdi nulisdvnv dry creek church anoseho yosewuna nuninetliyvda yigehe dudov nelvgi indian day church yidudoe indian day school ina tsigehv
segments.translation: I had a short walk to school. You could see it where I grew up. Indian Day was the name of that school. Have you heard of it, Indian Day? The building is still there, that old school and where the teachers used to live, the building is still there, but it is a church now where the school used to be. Dry Creek Church they call it. It would have been good if they didn’t change the name and called it Indian Day Church, since it was Indian Day School.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏴᏛᏂ ᎠᏯ ᏥᎦ Richard ᏓᏩᏙᎢ ᏙᎨᎲ ᎠᏎᏃ Guy ᎬᏬᏎᎰ Guy Soldier
segments.transliteration: vv yvdvni aya tsiga Richard dawadoi dogehv aseno Guy gvwoseho Guy Soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, say for instance my name is really Richard, but they just call me Guy Soldier.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Guy?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏂᎾᎭ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎡᏣᏁᎸ ᏱᎨᎮ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ?
segments.transliteration: ninaha tla gohusdi etsanelv yigehe sgi yusdi?
segments.translation: What about you, you weren't given anything like that?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏣᎵᏛ ᏥᎬᏬᏎᎲ ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᏣᎵ ᏣᎳᎩᏭ ᏱᎬᏁᎳ Charley ᏣᎵ ᏂᎦᏓ Ꭴ ᎮᏂ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏣᏁᎲ ᎤᎾ Dry Creek ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏬᏂᏍᎩ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎮᏍᏓ ᏳᎾᎵᏑᏰ ᎰᏩ ᏲᏁᎩ ᎠᏂᏬᏂᏍᎩ ᏣᎳᎩᎭ ᎮᏂ ᏙᏣᏘᏲᎯᎲ
segments.transliteration: tsalidv tsigvwosehv aniyvwiya tsali tsalagiwu yigvnela Charley tsali nigada u heni yusdi tsanehv una Dry Creek aniyvwiya tsigehv tsalagiha heni aniwonisgi tsigehv hesda yunalisuye howa yonegi aniwonisgi tsalagiha heni dotsatiyohihv
segments.translation: People just called me Tsali, Cherokee for Charley. Just about all those natives around Dry Creek spoke in Cherokee. There was not hardly any mixed in that spoke English. We argued around in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y'all fought in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, they didn’t give you a different name?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: No, just the same, Mel.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You had the same name?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: They just called me Mel.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏔ ᎠᎩᎩᏒ Guy ᏓᏩᏙᎥ ᏥᎩ ᎠᏎᎾ ᏍᎩ ᏂᎬᎩᏪᏎᎲ ᎠᏩᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᏃᎴ ᏥᏕᎦᏕᎶᏆᏍᎬ ᎠᏂᏲᏁᎩ ᏍᏊ Guy ᏥᎬᏬᏎᎲ Guy ᏥᎬᏬᏎᎲ yeah Ꮭ ᎠᎸᎯᏳ ᏱᎬᎩᏃᏎᎴ ᎠᎩᎩᏒ ᏍᎩᎾ Guy ᎾᎾᎭ ᏗᏨᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᏒ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎩᏗ ᎤᏂᏃᎮᏢᏅ ᏱᎨᏎ ᎨᏣᏃᏎᎸ ᏱᎨᏎ?
segments.transliteration: aya heni tla yawanvta agigisv Guy dawadov tsigi asena sgi nigvgiwesehv awadvsidisv nole tsidegadeloquasgv aniyonegi squu Guy tsigvwosehv Guy tsigvwosehv yeah tla alvhiyu yigvginosele agigisv sgina Guy nanaha ditsvgvyvlige tsigesv tla gohusdi usquanigidi uninohetlvnv yigese getsanoselv yigese?
segments.translation: Yeah, I don’t know where I got the name Guy, that’s just what they called me growing up and when I was going to school the whites called me Guy. They called me Guy; they never told me where I got Guy from… What about your parents did they ever tell you anything interesting?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏧᏛᎴᏅᏗᏛ ᎬᎩᏃᏎᎸᎾ ᎨᏒ ᎠᏎᏃ ᎠᏮᎨᏒᏃ ᎡᎵ ᎮᏂ ᎪᎯᎦ ᏙᎬᏩᏂᏲᎱᏒ ᎯᎮᏅ ᎤᏩᏌ ᎣᏍᏓᏘᏲᎯᎰ yeah ᏳᏓᎭᎡ ᏯᏂᏃᎲᎵ ᏯᎾᏛᏛᎲᎩ ᏥᎨ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏪᏘ ᏧᏂᎶᏐ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏯᏂᏃᎲᎵ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮎ trail of tears
segments.transliteration: tsudvlenvdidv gvginoselvna gesv aseno awvgesvno eli heni gohiga dogvwaniyohusv hihenv uwasa osdatiyohiho yeah yudahae yaninohvli yanadvdvhvgi tsige gohusdi uweti tsuniloso yudaha yaninohvli tsigehv na trail of tears
segments.translation: They told me different things, but I have forgotten, it has been a long time. It's been a long time since they passed. I just argue with this one now. Yeah, sometimes they would talk and remember something old where they came from sometimes. They would talk about the Trail of Tears.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s it!

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎤᏲᎡ ᏂᎨᎬᏁᎴ ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᎤᎾᎦᏐᏣᏁᏗᏭ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎨᏥᎢᎶᏞᎢ ᏯᎾᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏧᏂᎵᏍ ᎠᎮ ᎠᏁᎴ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: uyoe nigegvnele aniyvwiya unagasotsanediwu elisda getsiilotlei yanadi tsigehv sgina tsunilis ahe anele nahiyu tsigehv
segments.translation: The natives were treated bad; they were driven here like goats, they would say. I guess their grandparents were a part of that back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was sad what they went through.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Yeah, ᏍᎨ ᏱᎬᎩᏪᏎ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏙᎮᏂ Ꮟ ᎩᎶ ᏥᎦ ᏍᎩ ᏱᏁᎬᏁᎳ ᎡᎳᏓ ᏰᎩᎢᎴᎾ Ꮲ ᎢᎦᏓ ᎮᏂ Ꮭ ᏳᏫᎦᏗᎷᎦ Ꮲ ᎮᏂ ᏅᏃᎱᏟᏗ ᏱᏗᎳᎨ ᏑᎵ ᏯᎾᎵᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ
segments.transliteration: Yeah, sge yigvgiwese tsigehv doheni si gilo tsiga sgi yinegvnela elada yegiilena tlv igada heni tla yuwigadiluga tlv heni nvnohutlidi yidilage suli yanalisdayvhvsgi
segments.translation: They used to tell me that, yeah. Even if they done that to us, if we were driven somewhere today some of us would not make it there. We would be scattered on the road; buzzards would be eating.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏂᎾᎭ Ꮲ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎨᏣᏃᏎᎸ ᏱᎨᎮ ᏗᏣᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎩᏗ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ?
segments.transliteration: ninaha tlv gohusdi getsanoselv yigehe ditsagayvlige usquanigidi gohusdi?
segments.translation: What about you? Did your parents tell you anything interesting?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᎡᎵ ᏍᏊ ᎠᎩᏃᏎᎸᏁᎸ ᎨᎲ ᎡᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ
segments.transliteration: vv eli squu aginoselvnelv gehv elisi tsigehv sgina
segments.translation: My grandmother has told me about some things.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏯᏛᏂ ᏧᎾᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᏴᏫ ᏥᎩᎵ ᎴᏱᎦ ᏧᏂᎪᎲ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ?
segments.transliteration: yadvni tsunasdi aniyvwi tsigili leyiga tsunigohv tla gohusdi?
segments.translation: For instance, little people or ghosts that they have seen, did they tell you about it?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎪᎯᎩᏴ ᏥᎧᏃᎮᏍᎬ ᎡᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎩᎶ ᏧᏂᏲᏠᏎ ᎠᎮ ᎨᎮ ᏑᏓᏁᎳ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᎠᎨᏯᏅ ᎾᏅ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᎤᏥ ᎨᎮ ᏢᎾ ᏗᎾᎵᏍᎩᏍᎬ Ꮎ ᎠᏂᏴᏫᏯ ᏣᏅᎵᏍᎩᏍᎪ ᎤᏁᏅᏍᎡ ᎠᏓᏟᏕ ᏅᎮ ᎨᎮ Ꮎ ᎠᎨᏯ ᎾᏅ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ Ꮭ ᏳᏓᎸᏆᏕ Ꮎ ᎤᏥ ᎠᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᎠᏓᎨᏗᎮ ᎤᏪᏅᏍᏗ Ꮎ ᎠᎨᏯ ᎮᏍᏗ ᏤᏅᏓ ᎢᏗᏁᏍᏗᏭ ᎠᏗᎮ ᏙᏅ Ꮲ ᏳᏬᎯᏳᏁ ᎤᏪᏅᏎ ᎾᎾ ᎠᎬᏴᎵᎨ ᎨᎲ Ꮎ ᎤᏪᏥ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᎤᏁᎳᎦ ᏪᎾ ᎠᏓᏙᏎᎮ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏪᏅᏎ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏗᎾᎵᏍᎩᏍᎬ I mean Ꮎ ᎠᎨᏯ ᎤᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎦ ᎤᏪᏅᏎ ᎤᎵᏍᎩᏒᏎ ᏍᎩᏃ ᏚᏂᏢᏂᏙᎴ ᏃᎾ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᎤᏥ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ ᏭᎾᏏᏁ ᎤᏖ ᏂᏗᏛᏁᎵᏒ Ꮎ ᎤᏥ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎠᏍᎦᎨ Ꮎ ᎤᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎦ ᎤᏪᏅᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏭᎩᏒᏁ Ꮓ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏛᏅᏙᏗ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎾᏅ ᏙᏗ ᏣᏃᏎ fireplace
segments.transliteration: gohigiyv tsikanohesgv elisi tsigehv gilo tsuniyotlose ahe gehe sudanela asgaya ageyanv nanv asgaya utsi gehe tlvna dinalisgisgv na aniyvwiya tsanvlisgisgo unenvse adatlide nvhe gehe na ageya nanv agayvlige tla yudalvquade na utsi age sgina asgaya adagedihe uwenvsdi na ageya hesdi tsenvda idinesdiwu adihe donv tlv yuwohiyune uwenvse nana agvyvlige gehv na uwetsi asgaya unelaga wena adadosehe na agayvlige sgina uwenvse na agayvlige dinalisgisgv I mean na ageya usdayvhvsga uwenvse ulisgisvse sgino dunitlvnidole nona asgaya utsi asgaya wunasine ute nididvnelisv na utsi sgina yusdi asgage na usdayvhvsga uwenvsdi sgina wugisvne no gohusdi udvnvdodi na agayvlige nanv dodi tsanose fireplace
segments.translation: My grandmother was talking about, long time ago, someone was having family trouble. A man and a woman and the man’s mother. There was a dance somewhere where the natives dance and they went and the woman was running around on him. The old woman did not like her, that man's mother. The man did not want to let the woman go. “Don’t go! Let's just stay home,” he was saying. She didn’t obey; she went anyways. The old woman, the man's mother was saying, “Let her go,” she was telling him. So she went, his wife, she went to dance and then they just went to sleep, the man and his mother. The man laid down, he knew what his mother was going to do, that’s why he was forbidding his wife to go. She went and got some things that she was going to use, that old woman. What do they call fireplace?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Godi (fireplace).

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎪᏗ ᏍᎩᎾᎾ ᎤᎾᏅ ᎾᎠ ᏫᏗᎧᏂᏩᎾᏩᏕᎨ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎪᎯᏂᏴ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏃᏴᎵᏍᎡ ᎤᎵᏒᎵᏓᏁ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎤᎾ ᏭᏴᏞ ᎤᎾ Ꮎ ᎪᏗ ᎾᏅ ᎠᎵᏍᎩᏍᎬ ᎠᏓᏟᏒ ᎤᎾ Ꮕ ᎤᏲᎱᏎ Ꮎ ᎠᎨᏯ ᎤᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎦ ᏏᎾ ᏭᏬᏞ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎪᎯᏴ ᎤᎷᏥᏞ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏃᏴᎵᏎ Ꮓ ᎤᎷᏥᏟᏃ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ Ꮎ ᎤᎮ ᎾᏅ ᎤᎳᏗᏥᏟ ᏓᏫᏍᎦᎵ Ꮕ ᎤᏩᏰ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎠᏗᏍᎬ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏭᏂᎩᏍᏛᏁ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏛᎮ ᎤᏬᏎᎴ Ꮎ ᎠᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎤᏂᎩᏎ Ꮎ ᏓᏫᏍᎦᎵ ᎢᎤᎷᏥᏟᏂ Ꭷ ᏂᎾᏛᎩᎢᏛ ᎩᎾᏚᎵᏍᎬᎢ ᎠᎪᎮᎴ ᎠᎫᎢᎶᎡ Ꮓ ᏓᏫᏍᎬᎵ ᎠᏬᏎ ᎨᎲ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏘ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏘ Ꮩ ᏱᏅᎵᏍᏓᏂᏙᎵ ᎠᏎᏃ ᏍᎩ ᏯᎩᏪᏎ ᎨᎲ ᎬᎩᏃᏎᎲ. ᎤᏂᏍᎦᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏗᏍᎩ ᎨᎲ ᎡᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: godi sginana unanv naa widikaniwanawadege na agayvlige gohiniyv gohusdi unoyvlise ulisvlidane elisda una wuyvtle una na godi nanv alisgisgv adatlisv una nv uyohuse na ageya usdayvhvsga sina wuwotle na agayvlige gohiyv ulutsitle elisda gohusdi unoyvlise no ulutsitlino gohusdi na uhe nanv uladitsitli dawisgali nv uwaye na agayvlige adisgv sgina wunigisdvne gohusdi dvhe uwosele na agayvlige sgina unigise na dawisgali iulutsitlini ka ninadvgiidv ginadulisgvi agohele aguiloe no dawisgvli awose gehv tla yawati tla yawati do yinvlisdanidoli aseno sgi yagiwese gehv gvginosehv. unisgasdi gehv adisgi gehv elisi tsigehv
segments.translation: Fireplace, that old woman she was kneeling down near there. After a while something made a sound, it seemed like in the fireplace, and went up. While that woman was dancing and running, she died, that woman, his wife. The old woman was still sitting over there, after a while she seemed to come back. Something made a noise. When she came back, she had something sitting there, something fell in there, a piece of flint. The old lady had it laying there and it walked, I guess. The old woman said something to it, and it walked and when it came back, she told it “Now we did what we wanted to do” and she washed it off, that sanding tool. She told me I don’t know if it really happened, but that is what she used to tell me. They were mighty, grandmother used to say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏌᏭ ᏳᏩᎩᏗᏛ ᏗᎨᎬ ᏗᏝ ᎤᏕᎵᎬ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏧᎸᏫᏍᏓᏁ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏍᎦᏯ Ꮕ ᎤᎷᏨ ᎠᏎᏃ ᎤᏑᎵᎪᏨ ᎨᎲ ᎠᎵᏥᏙᎲᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏄᎵᏍᏛᏅ ᏍᎩ ᎾᏛᏁ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎪᏢᏅᏍᎩ ᎡᎵᏭᎨ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏱᏍᏉᏢᎾᏏ ᎠᎦᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ ᎠᏩᏂᎩᏌ ᎠᏂᎦ ᎡᎵᏭᎨ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏱᏍᏉᏢᎾᏏ ᎠᏬᏎᎸ ᏣᏗᎲ. ᏗᎪᎦᏍᏗ ᏍᎪᏅ ᏕᎯᏁ ᏥᏲᏎᎸ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎥᎥ ᎠᏭᏗᏝ ᏩᎩᏴᏢ ᏣᏗᎲ ᏩᏩᎵᏍᏛᏢᏅᏭ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎾᎾ ᏗᎪᎦᏍᏗ ᏫᏓᏬᎦᏍᏛᏅ ᏣᏗᎲ ᏢᏃ ᎯᏍᎩᎭ ᏯᏛᏬᏍᏛᏅ Ꮓ ᏩᎩᏴᏢ. ᎯᏛ ᏱᏦᎦᏍᏛᎾ ᏥᏲᏎᎸ ᏣᏗᎲ ᏱᏛᎦᎷᏥᏅ ᏛᎦᎷᏣ ᏥᏲᏎᎸ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎬᎵᎡᎵᏥᏍᎢ ᎤᏛᏅ ᎤᏂᎩᏒ ᏣᏗᎲ ᏔᎵ ᏳᎾᏙᏛᏩᏍᏗ ᏃᎴ ᎤᎷᏨ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎡᎷᎨ ᏴᏍᏉᏢᎾᏍᎠ ᏙᎲᎤᏍᏗ ᏥᏲᎮᎸ ᏙᎯᏯᏛ ᎤᎵᏍᎦᏂᏏᎠ ᎤᏂᎩᏍᏗ ᏥᏍᏉᏢᎾᏍᎠ. ᎤᏣᎬᏂᏏ ᎨᎮ
segments.transliteration: sawu yuwagididv digegv ditla udeligv sgi yusdi tsulvwisdane gehv asgaya nv ulutsv aseno usuligotsv gehv alitsidohvsgi heni nulisdvnv sgi nadvne gohusdi gotlvnvsgi eliwuge gohusdi yisquotlvnasi agasdayvhvsgi awanigisa aniga eliwuge gohusdi yisquotlvnasi awoselv tsadihv. digogasdi sgonv dehine tsiyoselv tsadihv vv awuditla wagiyvtlv tsadihv wawalisdvtlvnvwu tsadihv nana digogasdi widawogasdvnv tsadihv tlvno hisgiha yadvwosdvnv no wagiyvtlv. hidv yitsogasdvna tsiyoselv tsadihv yidvgalutsinv dvgalutsa tsiyoselv tsadihv gvlielitsisi udvnv unigisv tsadihv tali yunadodvwasdi nole ulutsv tsadihv eluge yvsquotlvnasa dohvusdi tsiyohelv dohiyadv ulisganisia unigisdi tsisquotlvnasa. utsagvnisi gehe
segments.translation: One time where I come from, to the west, he used to work like that. A man came but he had quit, he had become a preacher, making stuff like that. “Can you make me something? My wife left me, she left. Can you make me something for her to come back?” “’Do you have some smokes? I told him”, he said. “Yeah.” “Go in there and just sit down,” he said. “I will just smoke them smokes” he said. About five minutes later he came back in, “If you smoke this,” he said, “if she is going to come back, she is going to come back.” “I appreciate you!” he said. Then he left, he said. Two weeks later the man came back again. He said, “Can you make me something again?” “What is it?” the man told him. “She really is whiny… can you make me something for her to leave again?” he said. She was too whiny!

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: He didn’t want her there.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: He ran her off!

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎡᎵᏏ ᎮᏂ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏗᏓᏅᏫᏍᎩ ᎨᎲᏲ ᏅᏬᏘ ᏥᏈᏍᏓ ᏥᏍᏕᎸᏓ ᎠᏯᎸ
segments.transliteration: elisi heni tsigehv didanvwisgi gehvyo nvwoti tsiquisda tsisdelvda ayalv
segments.translation: My grandmother was a healer; I helped look for lots of medicine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᎲ ᏳᏖᏕ ᏱᎦᏕᎳᏆᎡ ᏙᎭ ᎡᎾᎨ ᎡᎯ ᏅᏬᏘ
segments.transliteration: dohv yutede yigadelaquae doha enage ehi nvwoti
segments.translation: It would have been good if I could’ve learned.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: It would have been good.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: Ꮭ ᏯᏘ ᏓᏫᏍᎦᎵ ᏭᎾ ᏍᏊ ᏳᏫᎬᏰ ᎤᎾ Ꮫ ᏓᏫᏍᎬᎵ ᏛᏴᏗᏱᎦ
segments.transliteration: tla yati dawisgali wuna squu yuwigvye una dv dawisgvli dvyvdiyiga
segments.translation: It might have been a piece of flint… It would have been a piece of flint!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎾᎾᎭ ᏗᏣᏕᏂᏙᎸ ᏏᎨ ᎤᏠᎤᏭ ᏄᏍᏗᏓᏂ ᏗᏣᏕᏂᏙᎸ?
segments.transliteration: nanaha ditsadenidolv sige utlouwu nusdidani ditsadenidolv?
segments.translation: What about where you used to live, is it still the same where you grew up?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: At Dry Creek?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏏᏛ Ꮎ ᎠᏫ ᏧᎾᏛᎯᏍᏙᏗ ᏚᏃᏢ ᎤᎾ ᏝᏯᏩᏘ ᏄᏰᏝᏛ ᏥᏄᎾᏛᏁᎴ ᏍᏈᏍᏓ ᏓᏁᎲ ᏴᏫ ᎤᎾ ᎩᎶ ᏥᎦ game reserve ᎮᏂ ᎠᏃᏎᎰ ᏚᏂᏅᎪᏫᏍᎣᏅ ᏂᎦᏓ Ꮭ ᏯᏩᏅᏔ ᏫᏄᎾᎵᏍᏛᏃᏅ ᏴᏫ ᎤᎾ ᎤᎾᏕᏅ ᎤᎾᏂᎩᏐᏁ
segments.transliteration: vv sidv na awi tsunadvhisdodi dunotlv una tlayawati nuyetladv tsinunadvnele squisda danehv yvwi una gilo tsiga game reserve heni anoseho duninvgowisonv nigada tla yawanvta winunalisdvnonv yvwi una unadenv unanigisone
segments.translation: Dry Creek, they have a place where they raise deer. I don’t know why they did that. There was a lot of people living there, it is a game reserve now, but they let everybody out. I don’t know what happened to all the people that lived there. They all left.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where you grew up, was there a lot of people that lived nearby?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎡᎵ Ꮫ ᏅᎩᎭ Ꮲ ᎠᎮ ᏓᏓᏁᎴ ᎨᎮ ᎾᎥ. Ꮲ ᏍᏊ ᏙᎯᏴ ᎾᎠ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎾᎠ ᏍᎩᏂ Ᏺ ᏓᏓᏁᎸ ᏍᎫᏂᎦ Ꭵ
segments.transliteration: eli dv nvgiha tlv ahe dadanele gehe nav. tlv squu dohiyv naa yigehe naa sgini yo dadanelv sguniga v
segments.translation: There were about four houses nearby, but they were not real close, but they were close that’s all.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you think back sometimes?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Sometimes!

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Your mind goes back thinking when you were growing up.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏥᎪᏩᏘᏍᎪᏭ ᏄᏍᏓ ᏄᎵᏍᏓᏅ Ꮎ ᏐᏈᎵ ᎤᏴᏍᏗ Ꮎ ᏦᎨᏅᏒ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᎮᏂ ᎮᎲ ᏦᎨᏅᏒ ᎤᏲᏝᎤᎥ limestone ᎦᏙ ᎤᏰᏍᏓᎥ ᎤᎾᏅ ᎤᎾᏓᏁᎸ ᎧᎵᏦᏕ ᎤᎾ ᎦᎸᎳᏗ ᎪᏢ ᎤᎾ ᎦᎸᎳᏗ ᎠᎦᏒᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏯ ᎠᏦᎸᏂ Ꮎ ᎦᏢ ᎤᏔᏂ ᎤᎾ ᎠᏬᏢ ᏌᎾᎴ ᏱᎦ ᎧᏬᏄ ᎦᏥᎦᏙᏍᏛ ᎠᎾᏓᏬᏍᎬ Ꮎ ᎠᎹ ᎤᏪᏴᏗ ᏍᏛᎩ ᎨᎲ ᎤᎾ ᎤᏙᏢᏒ ᏍᎨ ᎦᏅᏓᏗᏍᎪ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎦᎵᏍᏙᏗ Ꮭ ᏱᎬᏲᏩᎨ
segments.transliteration: tsigowatisgowu nusda nulisdanv na soquili uyvsdi na tsogenvsv amayutlidi heni hehv tsogenvsv uyotlauv limestone gado uyesdav unanv unadanelv kalitsode una galvladi gotlv una galvladi agasvsdi gehv aya atsolvni na gatlv utani una awotlv sanale yiga kawonu gatsigadosdv anadawosgv na ama uweyvdi sdvgi gehv una udotlvsv sge ganvdadisgo tla gohusdi galisdodi tla yigvyowage
segments.translation: I can still see where we used to keep the barn, our house was next to the creek. Our house, it was on a flat, the ground was on flat limestone, that’s where the house was. It had a high place, that’s where I slept. It had a big window. I would sit there early in the morning. I would watch the ducks swimming in the water; it was deep there. I remember that. There is no reason you could forget.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᏍᎩ ᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗᎰ ᏗᏩᏕᏂᏙᎸ ᏫᎡᏙᎰ ᎦᏓᏅᏖᏢᏍᎬ ᏳᏓᎭ
segments.transliteration: aya heni squu sgi nigalisdiho diwadenidolv wiedoho gadanvtetlvsgv yudaha
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what happens to me to my mind. It goes back to where I grew up.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏍᎩᏛ ᏱᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗ, ᏍᎩ ᎾᏩᎵᏍᏓᏁᎰ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏯ ᏳᏓᎭ
segments.transliteration: sgidv yinigalisdi, sgi nawalisdaneho squu aya yudaha
segments.translation: That’s what will happen, that’s what happens to me sometimes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Does the same thing happen to you?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᎤᏠᏱᏛ ᏍᏊ ᎾᏩᎵᏍᏓᏁᎰ ᏔᎵ ᏄᏙᏢᏒ ᏫᎦᏓᏅᏖᏍᎪ Ꮎ ᎠᎬᏱ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᏦᎦᏁᎸᏛ ᏃᎴ babo ᎾᎥ
segments.transliteration: vv utloyidv squu nawalisdaneho tali nudotlvsv wigadanvtesgo na agvyi amayutlidi tsoganelvdv nole babo nav
segments.translation: Yes, the same thing happens to me. I think about two different places, the first place we lived by the water and then near Barber.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You go there thinking about it?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: I can just see the things that have happened.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You have a beautiful vision when you think about it?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Yeah, beautiful… beautiful…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: boy, ᏙᏛᎭ ᏳᏓᎭ ᏩᏓᏖᏗ ᎨᎰ ᎾᎯᏳ
segments.transliteration: boy, dodvha yudaha wadatedi geho nahiyu
segments.translation: Boy, sometimes you just really have to think about it.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: You will miss it Yeah, you will miss it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you went there now, it has all changed.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎭᏗ ᏯᏓᏁᎳ ᎠᏯ ᎣᎦᏁᎳᏛ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ
segments.transliteration: hadi yadanela aya oganeladv gohiyv tsiga
segments.translation: Yeah, there is no building where we lived nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There's not?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᏃᎴ Ꮎ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᏦᎦᏁᎸᏛ ᎾᏭᏂ ᏗᎱᏣᏬᎵᏛᏗ ᏚᎵᏍᏔᏅ ᎤᏩᏏ ᎦᏝᎪ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏅᏱ Ꮎ ᏙᏳ ᏍᏊ ᏯᏩᏚᎸᎮ ᏗᎩᏲᎯᏍᏗ ᏥᏲᎮᎲ Charley ᎠᏎᏃ ᏧᏔᏂ ᏅᎧ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏅᏱ ᏗᏲᏢᏅ
segments.transliteration: nole na amayutlidi tsoganelvdv nawuni dihutsawolidvdi dulistanv uwasi gatlago tsigehv nvyi na doyu squu yawadulvhe digiyohisdi tsiyohehv Charley aseno tsutani nvka tsigehv nvyi diyotlvnv
segments.translation: No, and where we lived by the creek, the only thing left is the rocks that used to be the chimney, piled up. I would have wanted to bring those, I was telling Charley, but they were big rocks. They were carved.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, they were still standing there?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: Ꭵ ᏏᏛ ᎦᏝᎪ ᏧᏂᏲᏍᏛᏅ ᏧᏂᎲᏒ ᎮᏂ ᎦᎵᏦᏕ ᎤᎾ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᏦᎦᏁᎸᏛ Ꮎ ᎦᏚᏏ ᏧᏭᏂᏲᏢ Ꮓ ᏍᎪᎯᏥᏆ ᎮᏂ ᎠᎮ ᏳᏕᏘᏳᏗ ᎨᏎ ᏧᏂᎲᏒ ᏍᎩᎾ ᎦᎵᏦᏕ
segments.transliteration: v sidv gatlago tsuniyosdvnv tsunihvsv heni galitsode una amayutlidi tsoganelvdv na gadusi tsuwuniyotlv no sgohitsiqua heni ahe yudetiyudi gese tsunihvsv sgina galitsode
segments.translation: There is still a pile over there, they have been broken. They moved the house where we lived by the creek. They took it up the hill. That house was probably close to a hundred years old when they moved that house.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᏛ ᏳᏍᏗᏓᏁ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ Ꮟ ᎤᎾ ᏱᏙᏗᏁᎴ
segments.transliteration: dodv yusdidane gohiyv tsiga si una yidodinele
segments.translation: I wonder how it would have been if we still lived in those houses?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎤᏬᏚᏨ ᏛᎮ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎡᎵ ᎮᏂ ᏳᎪᏕ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᏬᏚ ᏱᏂᎬᏁᎵᏙᎴ
segments.transliteration: uwodutsv dvhe yigehe eli heni yugode gohusdi uwodu yinigvnelidole
segments.translation: It would have been beautiful. We might have put something there, made it more beautiful.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah…

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎤᏍᏗ ᏧᏓᏁᎸ ᎤᎾ ᎠᎹᏳᏟᏗ ᎭᏫᏯ ᎤᏍᏆᏂᎪᏙᏗ ᎡᎵᏏ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎤᎾᎾ ᏳᏩᎦᏍᎣᏌ ᎤᎾ ᏃᎴ ᎠᎹ ᎣᎩᎫᎩᏍᏗ ᏨᎨᎲ ᎣᏍᏓ ᎤᏬᏚ ᏥᎬᎾᏄᎪᎬ ᎣᏗᏝᏅᏗᏝ ᏗᏝ ᏳᏫᎠᎦᏐᏏ ᏃᎴ ᎤᏫᏒᏗ ᏧᏬᏢᏒ ᏍᏗ ᏳᏍᏗ ᏣᎧᏅᏢᏛ ᎤᎾ ᏃᎴ ᎤᎾ ᏃᎴ ᎤᏔᏂ barn ᏧᏓᏁᎸ ᎤᎾ ᎨᏓᎴ ᏂᎦᏗ ᏅᏃ ᎤᏲᏦᏅ Ꮓ ᏦᎦᏛᏅᏏ ᎦᏑᏏ ᎢᏃ ᏦᎩᎷᏥ Ꮓ ᏝᏗ ᎤᏠᏱ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎤᎾᎾ ᏦᎦᏕᏅ ᎡᎳᏗ
segments.transliteration: usdi tsudanelv una amayutlidi hawiya usquanigododi elisi tsigehv unana yuwagasosa una nole ama ogigugisdi tsvgehv osda uwodu tsigvnanugogv oditlanvditla ditla yuwiagasosi nole uwisvdi tsuwotlvsv sdi yusdi tsakanvtlvdv una nole una nole utani barn tsudanelv una gedale nigadi nvno uyotsonv no tsogadvnvsi gasusi ino tsogilutsi no tladi utloyi yigehe unana tsogadenv eladi
segments.translation: There was a small smokehouse where my grandmother would store meat. When you went off the hill there was a place where we dipped water. It was a good, beautiful spring. When you went down this way, he had a place for a garden, then it kind of went up the hill there. He had a big barn down the hill. It all fell apart when we moved from there. When we got to the top of the hill, it was not the same as where we used to live on the bottom.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏙᎲ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎢᎦ ᎠᏫᏒᏍᎩ ᎨᎮ? ᏎᎷᎨ ᏚᏯ
segments.transliteration: dohv usdi iga awisvsgi gehe? seluge duya
segments.translation: What all did he plant? Corn, beans?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎲ ᏎᎷ ᏚᏯ ᏄᎾ ᎢᎾ ᏒᎩ ᎢᎾᏅ squash ᏓᎹᏟ ᎢᎾ ᏧᎦᏂᏕᏂ ᎢᏅ ᏂᎦᏗᏂ ᏍᏊ ᎦᏝᏛᏅᏍᎬ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏍᎩᏳᏍᏗ ᎾᏅ Ꭱ ᎠᏥᎵ ᏣᏃᎮᎰ mustard green, turnip ᎢᎾ ᎣᏂ ᏙᏳᏅ
segments.transliteration: vhv selu duya nuna ina svgi inanv squash damatli ina tsuganideni inv nigadini squu gatladvnvsgv gohusdi sgiyusdi nanv e atsili tsanoheho mustard green, turnip ina oni doyunv
segments.translation: Yeah, corn, potatoes, beans, onion and squash, tomatoes, and cabbage. She canned all of the things like that and what they call fire mustard greens and turnips last.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏍᏊ Ꮫ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎠᏁᎲ ᏴᏫ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: squu dv nusda anehv yvwi nahiyu tsigehv
segments.translation: That’s just the way people lived back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s it.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏍᎩ ᏥᏂᏨᏛᏁᎲ ᏍᏊ ᎠᏯ ᏧᏓᎴᏅᏗ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏥᎦᏝᏛᏅᏍᎬ ᎡᏥ ᎨᏍᏗ ᎮᏂ ᎰᏩ ᏩᏩᎯᏍᏗ ᏱᎨᎮ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎣᏩᏌ ᎮᏂ ᎠᏛᎯᏍᏛᏅ ᎤᏂᎲ ᎨᎲ ᏄᎾ, ᏚᏯ Ꮕ ᏥᏔᎦ ᎢᎾ ᏚᏂᎾᏝᎥ ᏧᏪᏥ ᏗᏂᎲᏍᎩ ᏩᎦ ᎢᎾ ᎤᏅᏗ ᏧᏂᏁᎩᎡᏗ ᏚᏂᎧᎲ
segments.transliteration: vv sgi tsinitsvdvnehv squu aya tsudalenvdi gohusdi tsigatladvnvsgv etsi gesdi heni howa wawahisdi yigehe gohusdi owasa heni advhisdvnv unihv gehv nuna, duya nv tsitaga ina duninatlav tsuwetsi dinihvsgi waga ina unvdi tsuninegiedi dunikahv
segments.translation: That’s what we used to do, too. Mom canned various things, you didn’t hardly go buy things. You had what you grew yourself. Potatoes and beans, and they had chickens that laid eggs. They would have a cow to milk.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did they ever make cream?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really delicious.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: Butter ᎢᎾ ᎪᏢᏅ ᏙᏳ ᎤᏖᏗ ᏍᎩᏳᏍᏗ ᎣᏩᏌ ᎪᏢᏅ
segments.transliteration: Butter ina gotlvnv doyu utedi sgiyusdi owasa gotlvnv
segments.translation: And they made butter. It is delicious, that kind you make yourself.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎣᏩᏎ ᎪᏢᏅ ᏙᏳ ᏧᏃᏨᏯᏪᏍᏗᏲ churn ᏱᎦᏂᏗ
segments.transliteration: owase gotlvnv doyu tsunotsvyawesdiyo churn yiganidi
segments.translation: Made yourself, it makes your arms tired if you churn it yourself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah boy.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: Ꮲ ᏱᎩᏓ ᏣᎩᎲ ᎠᏯ Ꮎ butter ᎪᏢᏗ Ꮎ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎤᎦᏒᏗ ᏱᎦᎾᏗ ᏴᏙᏢᏍᎩᎢᏛ ᏙᏳ Ꮫ ᏧᏃᏣᏯᏪᏍᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮓ ᎦᎨᏗ ᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗᎲ
segments.transliteration: tlv yigida tsagihv aya na butter gotlvdi na gohusdi ugasvdi yiganadi yvdotlvsgiidv doyu dv tsunotsayawesdi tsigehv no gagedi nigalisdihv
segments.translation: I had one this big [gesture] to make butter with. It had that thing sticking out you did it like this [gesture]. When it was making it, it made your arms tired cause it got heavy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gawlee man.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: You can't forget about that growing up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: No, no…

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: lets see, ᏑᏓᎵ ᏛᎮ Ꮲ ᎣᏍᏓᎴᏂᎲ ᏩᎦ ᏙᏍᏗᏁᎨᎡᎲ ᎡᏙᏓ ᏙᏍᏕᏠᎲᏂ ᏌᎾᎴ ᏍᎩ ᏲᎩᏂᏍᏆᏛᏃ Ꮓ ᏠᎨᏏ ᏗᎦᎶᎪᏗ Ꮓ ᏗᎦᎶᎪᏗ ᏗᎦᏢᏗ
segments.transliteration: lets see, sudali dvhe tlv osdalenihv waga dosdinegeehv edoda dosdetlohvni sanale sgi yoginisquadvno no tlogesi digalogodi no digalogodi digatlvdi
segments.translation: Let's see, we started about six milking cows, me and dad in the morning feeding early, and when we finished that then to the fields to hoe and sharpen the hoes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Gawlee. ᎾᎾᎭ ᏗᏍᏗᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᏥᎨᎲ Ꮩ ᎤᏍᏗ ᏫᏍᏗᎸᏫᏉᏛ ᎨᎮ ᎠᎵᏍᏓᏗ ᎤᏬᏢᏅ ᎠᏓᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎬ ᏱᎦ
segments.transliteration: Gawlee. nanaha disdigayvlige tsigehv do usdi wisdilvwiquodv gehe alisdadi uwotlvnv adasdayvhvsgv yiga
segments.translation: Gawlee, what about your parents? What was y’all’s favorite food that they cooked?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎨᎲ ᏂᎦᏗ ᎠᎩᎸᏫᎩᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎪᏢᏍᎬ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ
segments.transliteration: aya gehv nigadi agilvwigidi gehv gotlvsgv gohusdi
segments.translation: As for me, I liked all of it what she made.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏙᎮᏂ ᎠᏂᏏᎾᏏ ᎨᎲ ᎤᎾᏓᏍᏓᏴᏗ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᎦᏴᎵᎨ ᎠᏂᎨᏯ ᏳᏍᏗᏭᏛᎨᎲ ᏯᏅᏂᏍᏓ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏛᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: doheni anisinasi gehv unadasdayvdi gohusdi anigayvlige anigeya yusdiwudvgehv yanvnisda osda dvgehv
segments.translation: They really were smart when it came to cooking, the old women and women. They would cook anything, and it would be good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, the table would be full.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏴᏴᏍᏗ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏴᎦ ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏄᏍᏓ Ꮎ ᎦᏍᎩᎸ sausage ᎤᏩᏨᏢᎾ ᏳᏝ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎡᏥ ᎩᎶ ᏳᏲᏏ ᎤᏴᏍᏓᏂᏓᏍᏗ
segments.transliteration: yvyvsdi gohusdi yvga sgi heni nusda na gasgilv sausage uwatsvtlvna yutla tsigehv etsi gilo yuyosi uyvsdanidasdi
segments.translation: You would grab something and eat it. That’s the way the table would be. She’d have fried sausage on there. If someone was hungry, they could just grab it and a biscuit, it would be covered up.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Really and…

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: A biscuit would be on the table.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᏄᏓᎴ ᏄᏍᏓ ᎪᎯᏴ ᏥᎦ ᏳᏩᏄᏢᎩ ᏭᎾ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏌᎾᎴ ᏯᎵᏍᏓᏃᏂ ᎪᎯᏅ ᏥᎦ ᏍᎩ ᏱᏂᎬᏁᎳ ᎤᏲᏛ ᏱᎦ ᎪᎯᏭᏯ
segments.transliteration: nudale nusda gohiyv tsiga yuwanutlvgi wuna tsigehv sanale yalisdanoni gohinv tsiga sgi yinigvnela uyodv yiga gohiwuya
segments.translation: It is different nowadays. They would cover it up after they ate in the mornings. If you did that now, it would go bad in just a little while.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would just throw it away.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: It wouldn’t be any good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏃᎴᎾ ᏥᏍᏓᏗ ᎪᎢᏛ ᏙᏛᏩᏗ ᏯᏝ ᎪᎢ ᏚᏯ ᎴᏱᎦ ᏱᏛᏝ ᎠᏃᏍᏗ ᎨᎰ ᏒᎯᏰ ᏱᎦ ᏚᏯ ᏃᎴ ᏣᏗᎲ ᎦᏚ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏧᏩᏄᏢᏍᎪᏭ
segments.transliteration: nolena tsisdadi goidv dodvwadi yatla goi duya leyiga yidvtla anosdi geho svhiye yiga duya nole tsadihv gadu osda tsuwanutlvsgowu
segments.translation: Like what y'all are saying that grease would be on the table all day and or beans, and they would still be good in the evening. Beans and bread, it would be good, they just covered it up.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎾᏍᏊ Ꭺ ᏙᎮᏂ Ꭺ ᎨᎲ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏥᎨᎲ it came from a pig you know ᎠᎾᏂᏍᏗᎲ ᎭᏫᏯ ᎠᎾᎵᏏᎾᏗᎲ Ꮎ Ꭺ ᏂᎦᎵᏍᏗᎲ biscuit Ꭴ ᎬᏗ ᏴᏒᏍᏗ ᏥᎨᎲ
segments.transliteration: nasquu go doheni go gehv nahiyu tsigehv it came from a pig you know ananisdihv hawiya analisinadihv na go nigalisdihv biscuit u gvdi yvsvsdi tsigehv
segments.translation: And the grease, it was real grease back then. It came from a pig when they would fry the meat, they would save the grease that it made. You could just mix it with a biscuit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Salt and a biscuit.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Salt and a biscuit.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᎡᏥ ᏥᎨᎲ ᎠᎵᏍᏕᎵᏍᎦ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏯᏛᏂ Ꮭ ᏱᏓᏂᎳᏫᎦ ᏏᏆᎠ ᏣᏅᏂᏍᏗᎰ ᎩᏄᏗ ᏱᏓᏂᎳᏫᎦ Ꮲ ᏱᏭᏓᏁᎯᎾ Ꭺ ᏣᏂᏯᏙᎯᎰ ᏨᎾᎵᏍᏕᎸᏓ ᎡᎵ ᎮᏂ ᎯᎢᎦ Ꭺ ᏣᎦᏂᏦᎯᎲ ᎡᏥ ᏥᎨᎲ ᏍᎩᎾ ᏥᎦᏗᏍᎬ ᏳᏓᏍᏓᏴᏂ ᎣᏍᏓ Ꮫ ᎨᏒ
segments.transliteration: aya heni etsi tsigehv alisdelisga tsigehv yadvni tla yidanilawiga siquaa tsanvnisdiho ginudi yidanilawiga tlv yiwudanehina go tsaniyadohiho tsvnalisdelvda eli heni hiiga go tsaganitsohihv etsi tsigehv sgina tsigadisgv yudasdayvni osda dv gesv
segments.translation: My mom used to help, say for instance, if they were having church and cooking a hog for their quarterly meeting. If there was any grease, they would give it out to the ones that helped out. She would bring this [gesture] much grease. She would use that when she cooked. It was good.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: You would be splashing it on beans.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I really like those beans. I would use a fork.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Smash them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then I would put grease.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: A hot biscuit.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏙᎯᏳᏛ ᎤᏖᏗ ᎠᎵᏍᏓᏱᏗ ᎨᎲ ᎾᎯᏳ ᎪᎯᏅ ᏥᎩ bologna ᏴᏮᎦ ᏏᏛᏲ ᏍᎩ ᏃᏍᏛᏛᏁᎰ ᎣᏍᏓᏓᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎪ ᎠᏯ ᏚᏯ Ꮫ ᏙᎩᏅᏂᏍᏙ ᏄᎾ Ꮕ ᏙᎩᏅᏣᏢᎶ
segments.transliteration: dohiyudv utedi alisdayidi gehv nahiyu gohinv tsigi bologna yvwvga sidvyo sgi nosdvdvneho osdadasdayvhvsgo aya duya dv doginvnisdo nuna nv doginvtsatlvlo
segments.translation: Food was really good back then. Nowadays we just go get bologna. We still cook like that. Beans will be cooking, and potatoes will be frying.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Yeah, ᎠᏯ Ꮫ ᏍᎫ ᎠᎩᏍᏓᏴᎲᏍᎩ ᏍᎩ ᏃᏍᏛᏛᏁᎰ ᎣᎩᏅᏏ ᏱᎦ ᏦᎩᎾᏓᎵᏏ ᎮᏂ ᎪᎩᎾᏝᏩᏍᏗ ᎠᏫᏴ ᏗᎾᏗ
segments.transliteration: Yeah, aya dv sgu agisdayvhvsgi sgi nosdvdvneho oginvsi yiga tsoginadalisi heni goginatlawasdi awiyv dinadi
segments.translation: Yeah, me and my wife still do that when we are by ourselves. Our grandchildren live with us. They are just ye tall [gesture].

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: We also have lots of grandchildren.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎣᎩᏅᏌ ᎮᏂ ᏱᏂᎩᎾᎵᏍᏛᏂ ᏴᏛᏄᏛᏴ water gravy ᏫᎪᏢᏍᎪ ᏃᎴ ᎦᏚ ᏭᎾ ᏗᏍᏓᏛᏅ ᎠᏭ ᏂᏗᎬᏁᎸ ᎦᏚ ᏓᏝᎲᏍᎪ ᎣᏏ ᎯᏛᏱᎩᏗ ᎦᏚ ᏙᏍᎫ ᎣᏍᏓ ᏗᎩᏍᏗ ᎨᎰ ᎦᏚ ᏍᎩ ᏳᏍᏗ
segments.transliteration: oginvsa heni yiniginalisdvni yvdvnudvyv water gravy wigotlvsgo nole gadu wuna disdadvnv awu nidigvnelv gadu datlahvsgo osi hidvyigidi gadu dosgu osda digisdi geho gadu sgi yusdi
segments.translation: When we are alone, just any time, she makes water gravy and bread made by hand. She just puts them on top, this big. They are good to eat, bread like that.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Yeah, they are good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᏳᏓᎭ ᎮᏂ ᏍᏊ ᏱᎦ ᏙᎪᏢᏍᎪ ᎠᎹ ᎤᏱᎦ ᏙᏍᏗᏍᏚᏟᏍᎪ ᏙᏍᏗᎩᏍᎪ
segments.transliteration: yudaha heni squu yiga dogotlvsgo ama uyiga dosdisdutlisgo dosdigisgo
segments.translation: Sometimes, that’s all she makes and we just put salt on them, and we eat them, yeah.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᎾᏛ fry bread ᏙᏳ ᏍᏊ ᎤᏖᏗ
segments.transliteration: nadv fry bread doyu squu utedi
segments.translation: That fried bread is really good.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎾᏛᎾ fry bread ᏱᎪᏢᎾ gravy ᎢᎾ ᏱᎪᏢᎾ ᎤᎾᏛ ᏴᎵᏍᏓᏴᎲᎦ ᏪᏌᏭ ᎡᎵᏍᏗ
segments.transliteration: nadvna fry bread yigotlvna gravy ina yigotlvna unadv yvlisdayvhvga wesawu elisdi
segments.translation: If you make that fried bread and make gravy, you can eat just like a cat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎾᏅ ᎠᎩᏲᏏᎲ ᎠᎴᏂ, ᎯᎾᎭᏃ ᎣᏂ ᏗᏝ ᏴᏛᎾ ᎩᎳ ᏗᎾᏛᏍᎦ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏣᏂᏬᏂ ᏄᏓᎴᏍ ᎤᏍᏗ ᎤᏃᏴᎪ ᏎᎾ ᏕᎦᏛᏏᏗᏒ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏥᏗᏬᏂᎰ?
segments.transliteration: nanv agiyosihv aleni, hinahano oni ditla yvdvna gila dinadvsga tsalagi tsaniwoni nudales usdi unoyvgo sena degadvsidisv atsalagi tsidiwoniho?
segments.translation: I am starting to get hungry. Now, this toward the last, for instance, the young people that are talking Cherokee: does it sound different then when we were growing up talking Cherokee?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It sounds different? How they talk now?

segments.speaker: mary-mccoy
segments.text: ᏄᏓᎴ ᎾᏩᎵᏍᏓᏁᎰ ᎪᎱᏍᏓ Ꭲ ᏳᏍᏗ ᎠᏝᎭ ᎾᏩᎵᏍᏓᏁᎰ ᎣᏂ ᏌᎶᎵ ᏣᎾᏗᎰ ᏌᎶᎵ ᎦᏗᎰ ᎠᏯ ᏱᎦ ᏌᎶᎵ ᏌᎶᎵ ᏯᏅᏓ ᏥᏍ
segments.transliteration: nudale nawalisdaneho gohusda i yusdi atlaha nawalisdaneho oni saloli tsanadiho saloli gadiho aya yiga saloli saloli yanvda tsis
segments.translation: It seems different to me, it seems like they put a "i" on the last when they say Sa-Lo-Li, I just say Sa-Lo-L, they will say Sa-Lo-Li.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Some will say Sa-Lo-Li.

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎥᎥ ᏍᎩᏛ ᏄᏍᏓ ᏳᏂᏪᏍᏗ ᎠᏂ ᏣᎳᎩ ᏌᎶᎵ it’s a squirrel ᏌᎶᎵ ᏥᏍᏚ Ꮕ ᏳᏂᎪ Ꮭ rabbit ᏱᎬᎾᏓ ᎨᎲ ᏥᏍᏚ ᏯᏅᏗ ᎮᏂ
segments.transliteration: vv sgidv nusda yuniwesdi ani tsalagi saloli it’s a squirrel saloli tsisdu nv yunigo tla rabbit yigvnada gehv tsisdu yanvdi heni
segments.translation: That is how the Cherokees would say, ‘it’s a squirrel’ [in English], ‘that’s a squirrel’ [in Cherokee]. And when they see a rabbit they won't say, ‘rabbit’ [in Cherokee], they will say ‘rabbit’ [in English].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: Yeah, rabbit ᏯᎾᏓ ᏙᏛ ᏚᏓᎴᎾ ᏙᎭ ᎯᎾᎭ ᏴᏛᎾ ᏔᎵᏍᎪ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᏳᏩᏟᎶᏢ ᎠᏱᏎᏍᏚᏭᏍ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎨᏒ ᏍᏕᎵᏍᎪ? ᏙᎨ Ꮲ Ꭸ ᏫᏛᎵᏒᏂ ᏍᏕᎵᏍᎪ?
segments.transliteration: Yeah, rabbit yanada dodv dudalena doha hinaha yvdvna talisgo tsudetiyvda yuwatlilotlv ayisesduwus tsalagi gawonihisdi gesv sdelisgo? doge tlv ge widvlisvni sdelisgo?
segments.translation: Yeah, they will say ‘rabbit’. There is a difference, ain’t it? What about this. Say for instance in about 20 years, do y’all think the Cherokee language will still be going, or do y'all think it will run out somewhere?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᎢᎠᎢᏎᏍᏚᏛ Ꮟ ᎾᎯᏳ ᏔᎵᏍᎪ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏓ ᎩᎶ ᏥᎦ ᎠᏟᎶᏢ ᏔᎵᏍᎪ ᏧᏕᏘᏴᏗ ᎾᎾ ᏕᎳᏆᏍᎬᏂ ᎨᎮᏍᏗ ᏅᎾᏁᏟᏗᏍᎬᏂ ᎨᎮᏍᏗ ᎤᏂᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎠᏂᏐ ᎲᏗ ᏱᎦᏰᎮᏍᏗ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎦᏬᏂᏓ ᏲᏁᎩᏛ ᏂᏓᎦᎵᏍᏛᏂ
segments.transliteration: iaisesdudv si nahiyu talisgo tsudetiyvda gilo tsiga atlilotlv talisgo tsudetiyvdi nana delaquasgvni gehesdi nvnanetlidisgvni gehesdi uniwonihisdi aniso hvdi yigayehesdi tsalagi gawonida yonegidv nidagalisdvni
segments.translation: If we are living in 20 years, when it becomes 20 years if they aren’t learning or trying to talk the Cherokees there will not be a Cherokee language. It will become English.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.text: ᎯᎾᎭ ᏥᏓᏅᏕᎳᏆ ᎡᏙᎮᏍᏗ Ꭸ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆᏍᎨᏍᏗ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎯᎾ ᏗᏂᏲᏟ ᏥᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆ ᎠᎢᏎᏗᏚᏭᏍ Ꮟ ᏍᏕᎵ ᎾᎯᏳ?
segments.transliteration: hinaha tsidanvdelaqua edohesdi ge gohusdi danadelaquasgesdi atsalagi hina diniyotli tsidanadelaqua aisediduwus si sdeli nahiyu?
segments.translation: What about this school where they are learning? Will it still be here, if they are still learning Cherokee, these children, do you think it will still be going?

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.text: ᏯᏛᏂᏍ Ꮎ sequyah ᏥᎦ ᏥᏓᎾᏕᎳᏆ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ? ᎤᎾ Ꮲ ᏳᎵᏑ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎩᎶ ᏍᏊ maybe an hour or two ᏱᎢᏗᎦᏬᏂᏗ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎬᏗ ᎡᎵᏍᏓ ᎤᏅᎨᏫᏍᏗ ᏂᎨᏒᏂ ᏙᏳ ᎮᏂ ᏫᏛᎵᏍᏆᏗᏟ ᎮᏂ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎢᎩᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ ᎠᏯ ᎮᏂ ᏌᏬ ᎣᎩᏂᎧ ᎠᏫᏄᏥ Tulsa Ꮲ Ꮺ ᏗᎧᏃᎩᏍᏗᏍᎦ ᎢᎦᏭᏅ ᎨᎲ ᏥᎦ ᎠᏁᏟᏗᏍᎪ ᏣᎳᎩ ᎤᏬᏂᎯᏍᏗ Ꭷ ᎠᎯᎵ ᎠᏕᎳᏆ Ꮎ ᏍᏊ ᏳᏪᏙᎳ ᏦᎩᏁᏅᏒ ᎦᏙ ᎥᏗ Ꭿ ᏱᎦᏪᏍᏗ ᎣᏍᏗᏃᏎ ᎰᏅ ᏍᎫᏭᏂ ᎬᏩᏘ ᎨᎰ ᏳᏪᏙᎳ ᏍᎩ ᎮᏂ ᏱᎾᏅᏛᎩ ᏯᎾᏁᏟᏗ Ꮎ ᏧᎾᏛᎾ Ꭵ ᏯᎾᏁᏟᏗ ᏧᏁᏲᏗ ᎾᏅ ᏍᏈᏍᏓ ᎥᎦᏛᎦᏅ ᏚᎾᏓᏟᏌᎲ ᏴᏫ ᎠᏂᏣᎳᎩ ᎠᏂᏲᏁᎩ ᎢᎾ ᎤᎾᎵᏑᏯᏩᏕᎬ ᏝᏅ ᏱᏙᎬᏁᏲᎲᎦ Ꮎ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᏳᏬᏝ ᎾᎾ ᎠᏲᏟ ᏳᎷᏥ ᎠᏫᏴ ᏝᏅ ᎯᏛ ᏁᏣᏪᏎᎠ ᏱᎬᏃᏏ. ᏲᏁᎦᎭ ᏱᎪᏝᎦ ᎠᏯ ᎨᎲ ᎠᏬᏟᏍᏗ ᎨᎲ ᏲᏁᎦᎠᎭ ᏱᎪᏝᎦ ᎠᏴᏫᏯ ᎠᏣᎳᎩ ᎢᎾ ᏱᎦ Ꮭ ᎮᏂ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏳᏅᏔ. ᏙᏳ Ꮭ ᎪᎱᏍᏗ ᏳᏅᏔ ᏱᎨᎷᏭᏂ
segments.transliteration: yadvnis na sequyah tsiga tsidanadelaqua anitsalagi? una tlv yulisu elisda gilo squu maybe an hour or two yiidigawonidi atsalagi gvdi elisda unvgewisdi nigesvni doyu heni widvlisquaditli heni tsalagi igiwonihisdi aya heni sawo oginika awinutsi Tulsa tlv we dikanogisdisga igawunv gehv tsiga anetlidisgo tsalagi uwonihisdi ka ahili adelaqua na squu yuwedola tsoginenvsv gado vdi hi yigawesdi osdinose honv sguwuni gvwati geho yuwedola sgi heni yinanvdvgi yananetlidi na tsunadvna v yananetlidi tsuneyodi nanv squisda vgadvganv dunadatlisahv yvwi anitsalagi aniyonegi ina unalisuyawadegv tlanv yidogvneyohvga na atsalagi yuwotla nana ayotli yulutsi awiyv tlanv hidv netsawesea yigvnosi. yonegaha yigotlaga aya gehv awotlisdi gehv yonegaaha yigotlaga ayvwiya atsalagi ina yiga tla heni gohusdi yunvta. doyu tla gohusdi yunvta yigeluwuni
segments.translation: Like, for instance, at Sequoyah where the Cherokees go to school, someone should be there to lecture them for an hour or two in Cherokee, so they don’t forget it. It is going to come to an end, our Cherokee language. We have a young boy, he lives in Tulsa. He is a musician. He really tries to speak Cherokee. He is learning. When he comes to our house, he will say, “How you say this?” We’ll tell him. He knows that when he comes over. That’s what they can do, if the adults try. If they would try to teach them. I have heard a lot about groups of Cherokee and white people mixed in, they will not teach them to be any different. If a Cherokee is sitting there and a child comes, they won't tell him, “That is what they are saying to you”, he will understand English. The way I understand it, if a Cherokee understands all English and if he is Cherokee, he doesn’t know anything. I would just think he doesn’t know anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I appreciate it!

segments.speaker: charley-mccoy
segments.translation: We appreciate it too!
